message.content:
Question: what is "pi-durable" (from Earendil, the company behind the Pi coding agent by Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher; released around October 2026, also a "pi-durable on Cloudflare" post), and how does its architecture differ from pi-coding-agent (the Pi terminal coding agent, packages pi-ai → pi-agent-core → pi-coding-agent → pi-tui)?

Report facts with sources (URLs), no recommendations:
1. What pi-durable is, in one paragraph, and which Pi packages it reuses or replaces.
2. Its architecture: where the agent loop runs, where session state lives and how it's persisted (event log? durable execution? checkpoints?), how tools execute (sandbox, remote, containers), how a client connects (protocol), how it survives crashes/restarts, how long-running or background work and multiple clients work.
3. Each concrete difference against pi-coding-agent's design (local process, JSONL session tree, extensions in-process with full permissions, four tools, TUI).
4. Trade-offs it states or that its docs/posts name: what it gains, what it costs (latency, complexity, infra, extensibility, permissions/security).
5. The Cloudflare deployment specifics (Durable Objects, Sandboxes, etc.) if documented.
6. Any diagrams or official terminology worth reusing.
Start from pi.dev, github.com/earendil-works, earendil.com posts, mariozechner.at, lucumr.pocoo.org, and the Cloudflare blog. Say which facts you saw in primary sources vs secondary.

Why Pi?

Pi is a minimal agent harness. Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around. Customize Pi with extensions, skills, prompt templates, and themes. Bundle them as Pi packages and share via npm or git.

Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub-agents and plan mode. Ask Pi to build what you want, or install a package that does it your way.

Four modes: interactive, print/JSON, RPC, and SDK. See OpenClaw for a real-world integration.

People of Pi: We've shipped Pi 1.0 with Pi Durable. Go make them yours.

Earendil Inc.

There are many agent harnessesbut this one is yours

Pi is a minimal agent harness.Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around.

curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | shpowershell -c "irm https://pi.dev/install.ps1 | iex"npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agentpnpm add -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agentbun add -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent

Why Pi?

Pi is a minimal agent harness. Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around. Customize Pi with extensions, skills, prompt templates, and themes. Bundle them as Pi packages and share via npm or git.

Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub-agents and plan mode. Ask Pi to build what you want, or install a package that does it your way.

Four modes: interactive, print/JSON, RPC, and SDK. See OpenClaw for a real-world integration.

Read the documentation

Change the harness, not your workflow

Pi isn't a sealed product. If you need a command, tool, provider, workflow, or UI tweak, just ask Pi to build it. It will customize itself on the fly.

Have Pi manipulate itself in place, hit /reload, and keep going. If you think others will find what you built useful, share it!

15+ providers, hundreds of models

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Azure, Bedrock, Mistral, Groq, Cerebras, xAI, Hugging Face, Kimi For Coding, MiniMax, NVIDIA, OpenRouter, Ollama, and more. Authenticate via API keys or OAuth.

Switch models mid-session with /model or Ctrl+L. Cycle through your favorites with Ctrl+P.

Add custom providers and models via models.json or extensions.

Tree-structured, shareable history

Sessions are stored as trees. Use /tree to navigate to any previous point and continue from there. All branches live in a single file. Filter by message type, label entries as bookmarks.

Export to HTML with /export, or upload to a GitHub gist with /share and get a shareable URL that renders it. Example session.

Context engineering

Pi's minimal system prompt and extensibility let you do actual context engineering. Control what goes into the context window and how it's managed.

AGENTS.md: Project instructions loaded at startup from ~/.pi/agent/, parent directories, and the current directory.

SYSTEM.md: Replace or append to the default system prompt per-project.

Compaction: Auto-summarizes older messages when approaching the context limit. Fully customizable via extensions: implement topic-based compaction, code-aware summaries, or use different summarization models.

Skills: Capability packages with instructions and tools, loaded on-demand. Progressive disclosure without busting the prompt cache. See skills.

Prompt templates: Reusable prompts as Markdown files. Type /name to expand. See prompt templates.

Dynamic context: Extensions can inject messages before each turn, filter the message history, implement RAG, or build long-term memory.

Steer or follow up

Submit messages while the agent works. Enter sends a steering message (delivered after current tool, interrupts remaining tools). Alt+Entersends a follow-up (waits until the agent finishes).

Four modes

Interactive: The full TUI experience.

Print/JSON: pi -p "query" for scripts, --mode json for event streams.

RPC: JSON protocol over stdin/stdout for non-Node integrations. See docs/rpc.md.

SDK: Embed Pi in your apps. See OpenClaw for a real-world example.

Primitives, not features

Features that other agents bake in, you can build yourself. Extensions are TypeScript modules with access to tools, commands, keyboard shortcuts, events, and the full TUI.

Sub-agents, plan mode, permission gates, path protection, SSH execution, sandboxing, MCP integrations (still supported alongside built-in MCP), custom editors, status bars, overlays.

Don't want to build it? Ask Pi to build it for you. Or install a package that does it your way. See the 50+ examples.

Bundle extensions, skills, prompts, and themes as packages. Install from npm or git:

$ pi install npm:@foo/pi-tools
$ pi install git:github.com/badlogic/pi-doom

Browse packages

and it can play doom

What we didn't build

Pi is aggressively extensible so it doesn't have to dictate your workflow. Features that other tools bake in can be built with extensions, skills, or installed from third-party Pi packages. This keeps the core minimal while letting you shape Pi to fit how you work.

Read the blog post

  • No MCP Now with MCP+Codemode

    MCP is built in, and Codemode lets agents compose tool calls in a JavaScript sandbox. MCP extensions are still supported too. Why we changed our minds

  • No sub-agents

    Spawn Pi instances via tmux, or build your own with extensions, or install a package that does it your way.

  • No permission popups

    Run in a container, or build your own confirmation flow with extensions inline with your environment and security requirements.

  • No plan mode

    Write plans to files, or build it with extensions, or install a package.

  • No built-in to-dos

    Use a TODO.md file, or build your own with extensions.

  • No background bash

    Use tmux. Full observability, direct interaction.

https://lucumr.pocoo.org/feed.atom Armin Ronacher's Thoughts and Writings Armin Ronacher's personal blog about programming, games and random thoughts that come to his mind. en 2026-11-23T10:31:40.586470+00:00 Armin Ronacher https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/11/9/irontown/ AI and Irontown 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00 Armin Ronacher For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.

A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.

The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns. He doesn’t take sides, but he wants to understand and find the truth. Another character is San (whom they call Mononoke), a girl who was raised by wolves and, despite being human, considers herself part of the forest.

This movie’s backdrop is human progress, and it reminded me so much of the challenges we are facing today with AI. AI is useful, empowering and consequential beyond the people who benefit from it. It’s similar to the iron in the story. Irontown gives the outcast purpose and power. There are people today who see themselves in an environment just like that: people who were never let in before and who can now build things that were out of reach. They are wielding AI to their benefit. But there are negative externalities. In Mononoke it’s not just the spirits and animals in the forest who bear the consequences, it’s also other people. Irontown produces guns, and its people are engaged in fights with other humans. There is conflict and power seeking everywhere.

Another, unseen character is the power-hungry emperor, who wants the head of the forest spirit, a god, because he believes it will make him immortal. Eboshi is willing to support that cause, not because she thinks it’s right, but because she is at war with the forest’s gods who are preventing her expansion, so they have a common interest. But there really is no need for anyone to kill the forest spirit, in the same way there is no need for any one country to “win at AI”. What drives it is the fear of what happens if someone else wins first. And the emperor is willing to have a god killed for it. The people who help him with that desire, Eboshi included, don’t understand the chaos it will unleash.

There it also shows the dangers of seeking overwhelming power without comprehension of how to control its consequences. The pursuit of power itself becomes destructive. In the end, the gods die, and what grows back is not the old forest anymore. Irontown is destroyed. Eboshi wants to rebuild it, and to build a better town this time. Ashitaka stays with the people of Irontown after his curse is lifted by the dying forest spirit. San cannot forgive the humans and stays with the wolves. In the end, nothing is truly resolved, but there is a truce that came at great cost.

Ashitaka’s role in the movie is one of a neutral actor. He was wronged both by a spirit turned demon in the forest, who put a curse on him, and, indirectly, by Eboshi, who caused the spirit to turn evil. Yet he harbors no ill will towards either side. He sets out to “see with eyes unclouded by hate,” and in the course of the movie he is seen as an unaligned actor. He helps people on both sides, and stands in their way to prevent further conflict. He doesn’t feel like a pacifist, but he’s the closest to one there is. He’s a truth seeker in a changing world. Because he engages he’s seen as suspicious by both sides, and ends up shot by the people of Irontown when he tries to rescue San.

I use AI every day and find it genuinely empowering. But I also recognize the pain it causes some, and the moral problems it poses. It’s genuine progress for humanity, but it comes at significant cost. And many of those costs will be carried by people who aren’t going to benefit from it.

So it’s no surprise that AI feels like a threat to many today. Communities currently strongly align themselves with one side and fight against the other. The forest spirit did not have to die and the boars did not have to die in a senseless war.

The question is not whether there will be iron, but what kind of Irontown we build with it. I want our conversation about AI to make room for nuance and genuine understanding, for us to look at it and each other with eyes unclouded by hate. We should take advantage of its real benefits, but also recognize the damage it can do, and the choices we still have about what we build and what we’re willing to sacrifice for it. I like to think there is a path for people with differing opinions can find a way to live alongside before losing something we can’t get back.

]]> https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/10/29/qwen3-custom-voices/ Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS 2026-10-29T00:00:00+00:00 2026-10-29T00:00:00+00:00 Armin Ronacher With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron crawler and we’re trying to learn a bit about game development along the way. However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we wanted to get a narrator and voice over.

But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which uses voice embeddings for custom voices.

With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it.

What Qwen Offers

Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We initially used Kokoro. However Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.

In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:

  • 1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
  • 1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
  • 1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description

The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.

At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.

Playing With It

For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI Conf, cut between two pauses so that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper. The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original recording.

Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother.

The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used 0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:

import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
    text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(),
    language="English",
    instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
    "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
    "aloud to a friend.",
)

You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Voice Embeddings

What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below).

Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices:

base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)


def fingerprint(path):
    prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
    return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding


def blend(a, b, t):
    a, b = a.float(), b.float()
    mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
    return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(
        torch.bfloat16
    )


armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")

Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice.

If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference:

import soundfile as sf

mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(
    open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed
)  # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")

The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file.

So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good does that work? I took an episode of State of Agentic Coding, the podcast Ben and I record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an embedding of me form the conference.

Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right.

On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For instance ECAPA, finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.

Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructed Cloned Voices

But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either (voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:

cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw)


def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
    ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
    told = [
        cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0] if instruct else None
    ]
    voice = {
        "ref_code": [None],
        "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
        "x_vector_only_mode": [True],
        "icl_mode": [False],
    }
    codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
        input_ids=ids,
        instruct_ids=told,
        voice_clone_prompt=voice,
        languages=[language],
        non_streaming_mode=True,
        **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
    )
    wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
    return wavs[0], rate


wav, rate = say(
    "I really thought this would work.",
    armin,
    "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.",
)

  post: ' Pi Durable | Earendil MENU Purpose Values Join Us Posts RFC Pi Radius Lefos Works Pi Durable Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 From: Earendil Engineering &lt; rfc@earendil.com &gt; To: You Subject: Pi Durable Today Earendil and the Pi community shipped Pi 1.0 . This reflects our belief that after countless hours of hardening, maintenance, and active development, Pi is now a solid foundation on which to build. Pi also continues to evolve. Together with Pi 1.0, we are shipping an experimental new package called Pi Durable. Pi Durable was built specifically for long-running, durable, and malleable agents that can run anywhere. We would like you to join in the fun and help us make it the best durable harness there is. Why Pi Durable? Pi the coding agent is built to run on your (remote) machine, inside a terminal, driven by one person. If the process dies, you look at what happened and tell it to continue. That is what Pi 1.0 focuses on and excels at, and that is not changing. At Earendil, we want to bring this technology to everyone, in whatever form fits their needs best. For that, we need a harness that runs anywhere, can be reached from different surfaces, supports infinitely long conversations, survives catastrophic internal and external failures, and lets multiple humans steer the same agents. Pi Durable is that harness. It does not replace the Pi coding agent. It is a framework for building any agentic application, coding agents included. It shares not only code with the Pi coding agent, like pi-ai, but also its principles: minimalism and malleability. It also lets us explore designs in this space without disrupting Pi the coding agent. Lessons we learn building agentic applications on Pi Durable will flow back into Pi the coding agent as they prove themselves valuable. What is a harness? Everybody has their own definition of a harness. We wrote about this previously , but let us reintroduce the concept of the harness for Pi Durable. A harness is storage plus the machinery needed to run one or more conversations with large language models in parallel. It provides the tools those models call, and the execution environments the tools run in. A conversation is an interaction between you and an agent, recorded as a transcript. The agent is the large language model together with its settings, like the thinking level, and the tools it can call. Tools do their work through an execution environment, which can be your laptop, a remote VM, or an in-memory sandbox. Which tools and which execution environment an agent gets is up to each conversation. Everything the harness runs, from calling the model to executing a tool, is a task. Like everything in Pi, Pi Durable is built so your agent can understand it. The entire source code, without tests, is about 15,000 lines, which comes out to about 150,000 tokens with GPT and about 250,000 with Claude. That\'s the worst case. To build on Pi Durable, your agent rarely needs all of it; the storage backends alone are 3,000 lines it can usually skip. Now let us give you a little tour of Pi Durable, to illustrate what we built and why we built it. Long runs anywhere We want agents to run for a long time and to be able to run anywhere, where anywhere currently means anywhere there is a JavaScript runtime. In Pi Durable, a harness opens over a storage backend. Pi Durable ships memory, SQLite, and JSONL storage, plus a conformance suite and benchmarks for your own backend. The SQLite and JSONL storage code uses no Node APIs, so with a small adapter it runs on Bun or inside a Cloudflare Durable Object. The storage interface is small and easy to implement on top of whatever you have, like a key-value store or Postgres. One process owns a storage at a time, and other clients attach to that process. On SQLite, the harness only keeps the working set in memory: the active transcripts, live tasks, and pending submissions. Everything else stays on disk until it is needed. Active transcripts are naturally bounded by the model\'s context window, because compaction summarizes older messages before they overflow it. So even a conversation with tens of thousands of messages fits snugly into memory. Tools that need files or a shell get them from an execution environment. Pi Durable ships a Node execution environment, which gives tools access to your local files. Like storage, the execution environment interface is small and easy to implement, so you can also expose remote execution environments to your tools. That allows the harness to run on one machine while its tools run on another. Your env function builds the environment for every tool call, from the conversation\'s working directory, so each conversation can run in a different place. import { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } from "@earendil-works/chord/context" ; import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/models" ; import { openaiProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/openai" ; import { createRegistry, Harness } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; import { NodeExecutionEnv } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/env/node" ; import { openNodeSqliteStorage, } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/storage/sqlite/node" ; import { CodingTools } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/tools" ; const context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT; // every call takes a context for cancellation const models = createModels(); models.setProvider(openaiProvider()); const registry = createRegistry(); registry.install(CodingTools); // read, write, edit, bash const env = ({ cwd }: { cwd?: string }) =&gt; new NodeExecutionEnv({ cwd: cwd ?? process.cwd() }); const harness = await Harness.open( await openNodeSqliteStorage( "./agent.sqlite" ), { models, registry, env }, context, ); // The root conversation: created on first use, and the same one after every // restart. const root = await harness.root(context, { agent: { model: { provider: "openai" , modelId: "gpt-6.1-sol" }, cwd: "/work/repo" , }, }); Survives crashes We want an agent to survive its process dying, whether the laptop sleeps, the container is redeployed, or the machine runs out of memory, and to pick up where it left off. In Pi Durable, every step of a run is a task that stores a checkpoint before it moves on. If the process dies, a new process opens the same storage, finds the unfinished tasks, and continues each one from its last checkpoint. A model request that was cut off is sent again; the partial answer stays in the transcript, marked as aborted. A tool call that was cut off reruns if it is safe to; otherwise the model is told it was interrupted. Pi Durable has no built-in subagents, but they take a few lines of code to build, as the triage tool below shows. A subagent runs in a conversation of its own, so it continues from where it left off too, and a subagent tool that is safe to rerun finds its subagent again and waits for its answer. Queued messages are still queued. A requestId makes a submission exactly-once, so a client that retries after a crash gets the original submission back instead of asking twice. const job = { type : "input" , content: "Fix the flaky login test" , requestId: "job-42" , } as const ; await root.submit(job, context); // The process dies here, in the middle of a tool call. // A new process opens the same storage. const harness = await Harness.open( await openNodeSqliteStorage( "./agent.sqlite" ), { models, registry, env }, context, ); harness.resume(); // continue the interrupted run const root = await harness.root(context); // the same submission, answered const settled = await ( await root.submit(job, context)).wait(context); Many conversations at once We want one harness to run many conversations at the same time, without one blocking another. In Pi Durable, one harness runs as many conversations as you need, concurrently, all with the same guarantees. A conversation starts fresh or forks another one at any point in its transcript, and sees the parent\'s history up to that point without copying it. Think of a Slack channel where your agent answers mentions from anyone. Then somebody opens a thread. The channel can be one conversation, and the thread a fork of it at the message the thread replies to. Both run at the same time and neither blocks the other. const channel = await harness.root(context); const question = await channel.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent why did the deploy fail?" }, context, ); const answered = await question.wait(context); // Someone replies to the agent\'s answer in a thread. Every conversation names // its owner, which decides what an abort reaches (more on that under Tasks). // The thread has none. const thread = await channel.fork( answered.answer!, { ownership: { kind: "ownerless" } }, context, ); // Both conversations work at the same time. const inThread = await thread.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent can we roll it back?" }, context, ); const inChannel = await channel.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent who is on call today?" }, context, ); await Promise.all([inThread.wait(context), inChannel.wait(context)]); Each conversation also stores its own agent: the model, the thinking level, the selected extensions and which of their tools are active, extra instructions, and the working directory in its execution environment. A reviewer next to the main agent can use a cheaper model, read-only tools, and its own checkout. Extensions We want everything an agent can do to be pluggable, and every plugged-in piece to take part in durability. In Pi Durable, an extension is a named bundle of system prompt sections, tools, hooks, and tasks. The application installs extensions in a registry. Each conversation selects which extensions and tools it uses, and stores only their names. System prompt sections The system prompt is rebuilt from the sections of the conversation\'s extensions before every request, so a changed section is picked up by the next request. Pi Durable records what changed in the transcript, at the position where it changed, so a restart or a fork sees exactly what the model saw. On models that support system prompt and tool changes in the middle of a conversation, only the change is sent, so the prompt cache stays valid. import { defineExtension, section } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const ProjectContext = defineExtension({ name: "project-context" , sections: [ // Read from the conversation\'s execution environment. The files can be // loaded and watched in the background; every request renders the // latest state. section( "agents_md" , (input) =&gt; agentsMd.latest(input.env)), section( "skills" , (input) =&gt; skills.latest(input.env)), ], }); Tools Every tool call runs as its own durable task, and its intent is stored before it runs. After a crash, a tool reruns only if it says that is safe. Otherwise the model is told the call was interrupted, with the output stored so far, and decides what to do. Each conversation can also get its own set of tools, like the Slack thread from earlier, which may search but not deploy. import { Type } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai" ; import { defineTool } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const searchIssues = defineTool({ name: "search_issues" , description: "Search the issue tracker" , parameters: Type.Object({ query: Type.String() }), replay: "safe" , // only reads, so a rerun after a crash is fine execute: async (args, api) =&gt; { // streamed to every client watching api.output( `searching for ${ args.query }\\n` ); return { content: [{ type : "text" , text: await tracker.search(args.query) }], }; }, }); const deploy = defineTool({ name: "deploy" , description: "Deploy a version to production" , parameters: Type.Object({ version: Type.String() }), // No replay: a deploy interrupted by a crash is reported to the model, // never repeated. execute: async (args) =&gt; ({ content: [{ type : "text" , text: await ci.deploy(args.version) }], }), }); registry.install(defineExtension({ name: "ops" , tools: [searchIssues, deploy] })); // The thread may search, but not deploy. await thread.configure({ tools: { remove: [deploy] } }, context); A tool gets the harness API for its call: it can commit entries and documents, start tasks and conversations, and talk to other conversations. That makes a subagent a few lines of code. A tool creates a conversation it owns, gives it a smaller model and its own instructions, and waits for its answer. The subagent is a conversation like any other, so it survives a crash, counts its own cost, and a UI can show it under the call. import type { AssistantMessage } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai" ; import { AssistantEntry, configure } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const triage = defineTool({ name: "triage" , description: "Label an incoming issue as bug, feature, or question" , parameters: Type.Object({ issue: Type.String() }), // a rerun after a crash finds the same subagent and the same submission replay: "safe" , execute: async (args, api, context) =&gt; { const child = await api.commit( async (tx) =&gt; { const existing = ( await tx.scanConversations({ ownerTaskId: api.taskId }, 1 ) ).items[ 0 ]; if (existing !== undefined ) return existing.id; // Owned by this call, so aborting the call aborts the subagent. const created = await tx.createConversation({ ownership: { kind: "task" , taskId: api.taskId }, }); // It starts as a copy of this conversation\'s agent. Make it a small // model without tools. await configure(tx, created.id, { model: { provider: "openai" , modelId: "gpt-6-luna" }, tools: [], instructions: "Answer with one word: bug, feature, or question." , }); return created.id; }, context); // lets a UI show the subagent under the call await api.details({ conversationId: child }, context); const subagent = await api.conversation(child, context); const request = { type : "input" , content: args.issue, requestId: `triage:${ api.taskId }` , } as const ; const settled = await ( await subagent!.submit(request, context) ).wait(context); // The answer is an entry in the subagent\'s transc'

Pi Durable

Date:Thu, 01 Oct 2026

From:Earendil Engineering <rfc@earendil.com>

To:You

Subject:Pi Durable

Today Earendil and the Pi community shipped Pi 1.0. This reflects our belief that after countless hours of hardening, maintenance, and active development, Pi is now a solid foundation on which to build. Pi also continues to evolve. Together with Pi 1.0, we are shipping an experimental new package called Pi Durable. Pi Durable was built specifically for long-running, durable, and malleable agents that can run anywhere. We would like you to join in the fun and help us make it the best durable harness there is.

Why Pi Durable?

Pi the coding agent is built to run on your (remote) machine, inside a terminal, driven by one person. If the process dies, you look at what happened and tell it to continue. That is what Pi 1.0 focuses on and excels at, and that is not changing.

At Earendil, we want to bring this technology to everyone, in whatever form fits their needs best. For that, we need a harness that runs anywhere, can be reached from different surfaces, supports infinitely long conversations, survives catastrophic internal and external failures, and lets multiple humans steer the same agents.

Pi Durable is that harness. It does not replace the Pi coding agent. It is a framework for building any agentic application, coding agents included. It shares not only code with the Pi coding agent, like pi-ai, but also its principles: minimalism and malleability.

It also lets us explore designs in this space without disrupting Pi the coding agent. Lessons we learn building agentic applications on Pi Durable will flow back into Pi the coding agent as they prove themselves valuable.

What is a harness?

Everybody has their own definition of a harness. We wrote about this previously, but let us reintroduce the concept of the harness for Pi Durable.

A harness is storage plus the machinery needed to run one or more conversations with large language models in parallel. It provides the tools those models call, and the execution environments the tools run in.

A conversation is an interaction between you and an agent, recorded as a transcript. The agent is the large language model together with its settings, like the thinking level, and the tools it can call.

Tools do their work through an execution environment, which can be your laptop, a remote VM, or an in-memory sandbox. Which tools and which execution environment an agent gets is up to each conversation.

Everything the harness runs, from calling the model to executing a tool, is a task.

Like everything in Pi, Pi Durable is built so your agent can understand it. The entire source code, without tests, is about 15,000 lines, which comes out to about 150,000 tokens with GPT and about 250,000 with Claude. That's the worst case. To build on Pi Durable, your agent rarely needs all of it; the storage backends alone are 3,000 lines it can usually skip.

Now let us give you a little tour of Pi Durable, to illustrate what we built and why we built it.

Long runs anywhere

We want agents to run for a long time and to be able to run anywhere, where anywhere currently means anywhere there is a JavaScript runtime.

In Pi Durable, a harness opens over a storage backend. Pi Durable ships memory, SQLite, and JSONL storage, plus a conformance suite and benchmarks for your own backend. The SQLite and JSONL storage code uses no Node APIs, so with a small adapter it runs on Bun or inside a Cloudflare Durable Object. The storage interface is small and easy to implement on top of whatever you have, like a key-value store or Postgres. One process owns a storage at a time, and other clients attach to that process.

On SQLite, the harness only keeps the working set in memory: the active transcripts, live tasks, and pending submissions. Everything else stays on disk until it is needed. Active transcripts are naturally bounded by the model's context window, because compaction summarizes older messages before they overflow it. So even a conversation with tens of thousands of messages fits snugly into memory.

Tools that need files or a shell get them from an execution environment. Pi Durable ships a Node execution environment, which gives tools access to your local files. Like storage, the execution environment interface is small and easy to implement, so you can also expose remote execution environments to your tools. That allows the harness to run on one machine while its tools run on another. Your env function builds the environment for every tool call, from the conversation's working directory, so each conversation can run in a different place.

import { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } from "@earendil-works/chord/context";
import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/models";
import { openaiProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/openai";
import { createRegistry, Harness } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";
import { NodeExecutionEnv } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/env/node";
import {
    openNodeSqliteStorage,
} from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/storage/sqlite/node";
import { CodingTools } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/tools";

const context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT; // every call takes a context for cancellation
const models = createModels();
models.setProvider(openaiProvider());

const registry = createRegistry();
registry.install(CodingTools); // read, write, edit, bash

const env = ({ cwd }: { cwd?: string }) =>
    new NodeExecutionEnv({ cwd: cwd ?? process.cwd() });
const harness = await Harness.open(
    await openNodeSqliteStorage("./agent.sqlite"),
    { models, registry, env },
    context,
);
// The root conversation: created on first use, and the same one after every
// restart.
const root = await harness.root(context, {
    agent: {
        model: { provider: "openai", modelId: "gpt-6.1-sol" },
        cwd: "/work/repo",
    },
});

Survives crashes

We want an agent to survive its process dying, whether the laptop sleeps, the container is redeployed, or the machine runs out of memory, and to pick up where it left off.

In Pi Durable, every step of a run is a task that stores a checkpoint before it moves on. If the process dies, a new process opens the same storage, finds the unfinished tasks, and continues each one from its last checkpoint. A model request that was cut off is sent again; the partial answer stays in the transcript, marked as aborted. A tool call that was cut off reruns if it is safe to; otherwise the model is told it was interrupted. Pi Durable has no built-in subagents, but they take a few lines of code to build, as the triage tool below shows. A subagent runs in a conversation of its own, so it continues from where it left off too, and a subagent tool that is safe to rerun finds its subagent again and waits for its answer. Queued messages are still queued. A requestId makes a submission exactly-once, so a client that retries after a crash gets the original submission back instead of asking twice.

const job = {
    type: "input",
    content: "Fix the flaky login test",
    requestId: "job-42",
} as const;
await root.submit(job, context);
// The process dies here, in the middle of a tool call.

// A new process opens the same storage.
const harness = await Harness.open(
    await openNodeSqliteStorage("./agent.sqlite"),
    { models, registry, env },
    context,
);
harness.resume(); // continue the interrupted run
const root = await harness.root(context);
// the same submission, answered
const settled = await (await root.submit(job, context)).wait(context);

Many conversations at once

We want one harness to run many conversations at the same time, without one blocking another.

In Pi Durable, one harness runs as many conversations as you need, concurrently, all with the same guarantees. A conversation starts fresh or forks another one at any point in its transcript, and sees the parent's history up to that point without copying it.

Think of a Slack channel where your agent answers mentions from anyone. Then somebody opens a thread. The channel can be one conversation, and the thread a fork of it at the message the thread replies to. Both run at the same time and neither blocks the other.

const channel = await harness.root(context);
const question = await channel.submit(
    { type: "input", content: "@agent why did the deploy fail?" },
    context,
);
const answered = await question.wait(context);

// Someone replies to the agent's answer in a thread. Every conversation names
// its owner, which decides what an abort reaches (more on that under Tasks).
// The thread has none.
const thread = await channel.fork(
    answered.answer!,
    { ownership: { kind: "ownerless" } },
    context,
);

// Both conversations work at the same time.
const inThread = await thread.submit(
    { type: "input", content: "@agent can we roll it back?" },
    context,
);
const inChannel = await channel.submit(
    { type: "input", content: "@agent who is on call today?" },
    context,
);
await Promise.all([inThread.wait(context), inChannel.wait(context)]);

Each conversation also stores its own agent: the model, the thinking level, the selected extensions and which of their tools are active, extra instructions, and the working directory in its execution environment. A reviewer next to the main agent can use a cheaper model, read-only tools, and its own checkout.

Extensions

We want everything an agent can do to be pluggable, and every plugged-in piece to take part in durability.

In Pi Durable, an extension is a named bundle of system prompt sections, tools, hooks, and tasks. The application installs extensions in a registry. Each conversation selects which extensions and tools it uses, and stores only their names.

System prompt sections

The system prompt is rebuilt from the sections of the conversation's extensions before every request, so a changed section is picked up by the next request. Pi Durable records what changed in the transcript, at the position where it changed, so a restart or a fork sees exactly what the model saw. On models that support system prompt and tool changes in the middle of a conversation, only the change is sent, so the prompt cache stays valid.

import { defineExtension, section } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";

const ProjectContext = defineExtension({
    name: "project-context",
    sections: [
        // Read from the conversation's execution environment. The files can be
        // loaded and watched in the background; every request renders the
        // latest state.
        section("agents_md", (input) => agentsMd.latest(input.env)),
        section("skills", (input) => skills.latest(input.env)),
    ],
});

Tools

Every tool call runs as its own durable task, and its intent is stored before it runs. After a crash, a tool reruns only if it says that is safe. Otherwise the model is told the call was interrupted, with the output stored so far, and decides what to do. Each conversation can also get its own set of tools, like the Slack thread from earlier, which may search but not deploy.

import { Type } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";
import { defineTool } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";

const searchIssues = defineTool({
    name: "search_issues",
    description: "Search the issue tracker",
    parameters: Type.Object({ query: Type.String() }),
    replay: "safe", // only reads, so a rerun after a crash is fine
    execute: async (args, api) => {
        // streamed to every client watching
        api.output(`searching for ${args.query}\n`);
        return {
            content: [{ type: "text", text: await tracker.search(args.query) }],

const deploy = defineTool({
    name: "deploy",
    description: "Deploy a version to production",
    parameters: Type.Object({ version: Type.String() }),

    execute: async (args) => ({

registry.install(defineExtension({ name: "ops", tools: [searchIssues, deploy] }));

// The thread may search, but not deploy.
await thread.configure({ tools: { remove: [deploy] } }, context);

A tool gets the harness API for its call: it can commit entries and documents, start tasks and conversations, and talk to other conversations. That makes a subagent a few lines of code. A tool creates a conversation it owns, gives it a smaller model and its own instructions, and waits for its answer. The subagent is a conversation like any other, so it survives a crash, counts its own cost, and a UI can show it under the call.

import type { AssistantMessage } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";
import { AssistantEntry, configure } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";

Extensions can also change other extensions' tools. A tool with the same name in a later extension replaces the earlier one, for example a bash that runs inside a Python virtualenv. A wrap decorates whichever tool won, wherever the wrapping extension is selected.

const Timing = defineExtension({

Subject:Pi 1.0

Today we are proudly shipping Pi 1.0: a hardened, minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own. Hundreds of thousands of people around the world use Pi every week. Many of you submit issues and pull requests. Over the course of many months, we have used that feedback to improve, harden and evolve Pi into a stable piece of software that people and businesses can depend on.

Pi is known for being minimal. We care about holding that line. While agentic tooling changes every week, many of the changes do not last. Pi does not work that way. We wait until something has proven itself, and only then do we consider adopting it; weighing its true functionality against its inherent added complexity. We spoke more about that process and how it relates to Codemode and MCP earlier this week here.

The Pi 1.0 we are shipping today is a result of that process. Pi already ran the latest models from every major provider, became a daily driver coding agent for people around the world, and provided a supermalleable substrate on which to build agentic applications. With Pi 1.0 we are adding the following into Pi:

  • Codemode (native support for MCP, and non-LLM models like Jev and image models)
  • Extension support for virtual models
  • Deferred tool loading
  • Cache warming for anthropic models
  • Mid-conversation system messages (transcript-aware prompt and tool changes)
  • A new TUI theme
  • Full-screen mode by default

We have thought about many of these features for months. They were thrown up against the wall and stuck. The list of things that fell off the wall is much longer. When we use Pi with all these new features it feels like a major step forward, but it also still feels simple, like Pi.

Alongside this work of continually refining and evolving Pi, we also began to understand that there were aspects of Pi that did not fit the shape of how many people wanted to use it. At Earendil, we want to bring Pi's minimalism and the way it allows you to wield AI outside of the coding agent and outside of the terminal. It needs to be reachable from different surfaces and support longer-running conversations and tasks. In short, Pi must become more durable. Rather than stray from our minimal roots and try to make Pi something it wasn't, we combined that work into a new experimental package that we are shipping today, Pi Durable. Pi Durable is a new substrate for building long-running agentic applications that lets the builders and the users of those applications wield and steer the underlying intelligence with tremendous dexterity. It shares Pi's key principles, minimalism and supermalleability, but it extends those principles into new dimensions. Mario writes in more detail about how we crafted Pi Durable here.

Earendil was formed to craft software and open protocols that strengthen human agency. Today we are shipping tools to you all to help do just that. We're eager to hear feedback from you and to harness the future out in the open together.

# pi-durable on Cloudflare

A working example of [`@earendil-works/pi-durable`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@earendil-works/pi-durable) running in a Cloudflare Durable Object.

Start with the [Pi Durable announcement](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/) for the ideas behind the harness. This repository shows one way to put those ideas into a small, usable web application.

Pi Durable is experimental, so its APIs may still change.

## What you can try

- Create a shared chat session and open it in multiple browsers.
- Run several conversations at once and fork a conversation from an earlier message.
- Reconnect without losing committed transcripts or queued prompts.
- Schedule one-time or recurring follow-ups.
- Ask a search subagent about earlier conversations.
- Open Activity to inspect live task ownership, waits, sleeps, tool calls, and background work while conversations run.

This is a sample, not a production service. It intentionally has no authentication or rate limiting.

## Run it locally

You need Node.js 22.19 or newer, pnpm 11, and an OpenAI API key.

```sh
pnpm install
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
```

Add your key to `.dev.vars`:

```dotenv
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key
```

Then start the Worker and React client together:

```sh
pnpm dev
```

Open the local URL printed by Vite, create a session, and send a message. Open the session URL in another browser to try the multiplayer flow.

## Where to look

The shortest path through the project is:

- [`src/chat.ts`](src/chat.ts) defines the models, extensions, tools, and default agent.
- [`src/session.ts`](src/session.ts) hosts the harness with Pi Durable's built-in Durable Object SQLite storage and connects it to Cloudflare's native hibernating WebSockets and alarms. Each socket watches one conversation's view (`Conversation.watch()`): the server sends its first value, then its changes as Chord operations, and pages older entries on request.
- [`src/tools.ts`](src/tools.ts), [`src/schedule.ts`](src/schedule.ts), and [`src/search.ts`](src/search.ts) contain the example tools and tasks.
- [`src/client/`](src/client/) is the React client. It applies the operations to each conversation's view, keeps the whole transcript with Pi Durable's `ConversationTranscript`, and renders the result: entries, and `pi.live` for the run, the streamed answer, tool progress, and failures.
- [`test/`](test/) covers application flows including restart recovery, scheduling, forks, and inboxes. Pi Durable tests its built-in Cloudflare storage adapter inside a Durable Object itself.

The code is the documentation for this integration. In particular, the tests are useful examples of restart behavior, scheduling, forks, and inboxes.

## Commands

```sh
pnpm dev        # local development
pnpm test       # test suite
pnpm check      # formatting, types, build, and deploy dry run
pnpm build      # production build
pnpm preview    # preview the production build locally
```

## Deploy

Authenticate Wrangler, store the API key as a Worker secret, then deploy:

```sh
pnpm exec wrangler login
pnpm exec wrangler secret put OPENAI_API_KEY
pnpm deploy
```

Before exposing a deployment, add authentication, authorization, and rate limiting. Anyone who can reach this sample can create sessions that use your model credentials.

## Further reading

- [Pi Durable announcement](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/)
- [pi-durable package documentation](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/durable)
- [pi-durable examples](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/durable/test/examples)
- [Cloudflare Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/)
