    "body": "### New Features\n\n- **Image input for classifiers**: codemode `models.classify()` accepts `images` for TypeSafe's Jev and Cloudflare's Clef models on `typesafe`, `cloudflare-workers-ai`, and OpenRouter. See [Use classifier models](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.4.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/models.md#use-classifier-models) and [Codemode](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.4.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md#models).\n- **Models Configuration reference**: every provider, model, model override, and compatibility field of `models.json`, generated from its schema. See [Models Configuration](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.4.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/models-configuration.md).\n- **Summaries without a fixed output cap**: compaction and branch summaries use the model's output limit, so long reasoning no longer makes them fail. See [Compaction](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.4.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/compaction.md#compaction).\n- **Codemode waits for a free worker**: parallel scripts and in-process subagents queue instead of failing, and `PI_CODEMODE_MAX_WORKERS` raises the limit. See [Codemode limits](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.4.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md#limits).\n- **Rex terminal support**: OSC 8 hyperlinks, truecolor, and inline images.\n\n### Added\n\n- Added a Models Configuration reference generated from the `models.json` schema, listing all provider, model, model override, and compatibility fields ([#10790](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10790))\n- Codemode `models.classify()` now accepts `images` for TypeSafe's Jev and Cloudflare's Clef models on `typesafe`, `cloudflare-workers-ai`, and OpenRouter, and lists Clef Omni and Jev 1.14 on Workers AI.\n- Provider-level `compat` in `models.json` now also applies to classifier models, with the System One fields `imageInput` and `sendImageOptInHeader` for proxies that serve another service's classifiers. Extension classifier models accept `compat` too.\n- Added `MiniMax-M3.1-Flash` to the `minimax` and `minimax-cn` providers, with thinking levels low through max ([#11121](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11121))\n- Added support for the Rex terminal: OSC 8 hyperlinks, truecolor, and inline images ([#11131](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11131), [#11150](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11150) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll), [#11183](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11183) by [@nihaals](https://github.com/nihaals))\n\n### Changed\n\n- Provider attribution headers now come from pi-ai's client identity. Extensions' `before_provider_headers` handlers no longer see the OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, and OpenCode attribution headers; returning `null` for one still removes it. Cloudflare requests send pi's detailed `User-Agent` instead of `pi-coding-agent`, as do GitHub release checks for tool downloads, and OpenCode requests send `x-opencode-client` whenever attribution is enabled, not only with a session.\n- `generateSummary()` and `generateSummaryWithUsage()` now ignore their `reserveTokens` parameter. Summary requests use the model's output limit instead.\n- Changed the default GitHub Copilot model from `gpt-5.4`, which Copilot retired, to `gpt-6.1-sol`.\n- Changed the default NVIDIA model to `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b` ([#10910](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/10910) by [@cv](https://github.com/cv))\n- Changed the default Xiaomi model to `mimo-v2.6-pro` for the `xiaomi` and Xiaomi Token Plan providers, since `mimo-v2.5-pro` left the catalog.\n- Grok 4.3 and Grok 4.5 on the `xai` provider now offer the `xhigh` thinking level.\n- Sign in with ChatGPT: ChatGPT Business workspace usage-limit errors are not retried and tell the user to ask their workspace admin to increase the limit.\n\n### Fixed\n\n- Fixed compaction and branch summaries failing with \"generation hit the token cap\" when reasoning used most of the fixed summary output limit. Summaries now use the model's output limit, and `compaction.reserveTokens` only controls when compaction starts ([#9512](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9512), [#9075](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9075)).\n- Fixed `models.schema.json` missing descriptions for provider and model fields, so editors showed no hints for them ([#10790](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10790))\n- Fixed `pi update` failing with \"Managed install marker is missing or invalid\" when `managed-install.json` starts with a UTF-8 BOM, which Windows PowerShell 5.1 adds when it rewrites the file.\n- Fixed HTML export showing literal asterisks for Markdown bold and italic next to CJK punctuation ([#3353](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/3353), [#10154](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10154))\n- Fixed the terminal staying in mouse-tracking, focus-reporting, Kitty keyboard, and alternate-screen modes when pi exits without its normal terminal teardown, which flooded the shell prompt with escape sequences ([#11170](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11170))\n- Fixed concurrent extension `select`/`confirm`/`input`/`editor` dialogs and inline `custom()` components in interactive mode: a second dialog replaced the first and the first promise never settled; closing the visible dialog now shows the previous one again ([#11166](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11166), [#9909](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9909))\n- Fixed pasting in the shell hanging after copying text in pi and suspending it with Ctrl+Z on Linux: the background `wl-copy`/`xclip`/`xsel` process that keeps serving the clipboard was suspended along with pi ([#11179](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11179))\n- Fixed codemode scripts failing immediately when both codemode workers are busy, for example with parallel codemode calls or in-process subagents. Scripts now wait up to 60 seconds for a free worker, and `PI_CODEMODE_MAX_WORKERS` raises the limit of two workers ([#11184](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11184))\n- Fixed extensions failing to load when importing `@earendil-works/pi-ai/models` (e.g. for `clampThinkingLevel`) by exposing the subpath through the extension loader aliases and virtual modules ([#11156](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11156))\n- Fixed `mcp.json` files that start with a UTF-8 BOM failing to parse, which skipped all their MCP servers and made `pi mcp add`/`pi mcp remove` fail ([#11191](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11191))\n- Fixed `/compact <instructions>` ignoring the instructions when summarizing the start of a turn that compaction splits. When the split turn was the only new content since the last compaction, the instructions were ignored entirely ([#11058](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11058))\n- Fixed resumed sessions and `/tree` navigation leaving extension tools inactive when the branch recorded its tools before they were registered, such as tools from extensions installed after the session started. Extension tools the branch never added or removed are now active unless they are registered with `defaultActive: false` ([#11062](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11062), [#11075](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11075))\n- Fixed sessions breaking after recovery from a response cut off at the output limit: the truncated tool call was omitted but its tool results were kept, so providers rejected every later request ([#11227](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11227), [#11233](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11233) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll))\n- Fixed the `grep` tool following `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, where options such as `--fixed-strings` silently changed regex searches into literal ones. The tool now runs `rg --no-config` ([#11203](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11203), [#11230](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11230) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll))\n- Fixed Windows shell detection rejecting runnable Microsoft Store shell aliases ([#9504](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/9504) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll))\n- Fixed Windows shell detection missing PowerShell outside `PATH` and the legacy WSL `bash.exe` launcher when Windows is not installed in `C:\\Windows`. pi now checks `%ProgramFiles%\\PowerShell\\7`, `%SystemRoot%\\System32\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0`, and `%SystemRoot%` ([#9501](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/9501) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll))\n- Fixed GitHub Copilot sessions with large request bodies, such as many images, failing with HTTP 413 `failed to parse request` instead of compacting and retrying ([#11016](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11016) by [@petrroll](https://github.com/petrroll))\n- Fixed the `openai-codex` provider offering `gpt-5.5` and `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`, which always fail for ChatGPT accounts ([#11173](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/11173) by [@lucasmeijer](https://github.com/lucasmeijer))\n- Fixed whitespace-only tool output (for example a bare `\\r\\n` from bash) making OpenAI Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Google requests fail with a 400 ([#8720](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/8720))\n- Fixed automatic retry not triggering for more gateway upstream failures, `stream disconnected before completion` errors relayed by Codex CLI proxies, and transient Google Vertex OAuth token refresh failures, and retrying errors because of digits inside request ids or byte counts ([#10920](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10920), [#11057](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11057), [#10996](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10996))\n- Fixed OpenAI Responses models losing the prompt cache on every deferred tool load after a tool was removed ([#10940](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10940))\n- Fixed Cloudflare Workers AI classifier pricing: Clef Flash costs $0.038 and Jev $0.042 per million input tokens instead of Jev being listed as free.\n- Fixed an unclosed `$$` display-math block swallowing or corrupting every Markdown table after it ([#11159](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/11159))\n- Fixed Markdown bold and italic not rendering next to CJK punctuation ([#10730](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/10730) by [@theBucky](https://github.com/theBucky))\n- Fixed `@` file autocomplete returning no results for queries containing regex metacharacters such as `[` or `(` ([#10972](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10972))\n",

  persist: '\n' +
    '## Persist and Resume\n' +
    '\n' +
    'Use SQLite or JSONL storage to keep conversations across restarts:\n' +
    '\n' +
    '```typescript\n' +
    'import { openNodeSqliteStorage } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/storage/sqlite/node";\n' +
    '\n' +
    'const harness = await Harness.open(await openNodeSqliteStorage("./session.sqlite"), { models, registry }, context);\n' +
    'const root = await harness.root(context); // the same root as last time\n' +
    'harness.resume(); // continue any run the last process left unfinished\n' +
    '```\n' +
    '\n' +
    "Work interrupted by a crash or close stays pending. `resume()` starts the task scheduler; submitting or waiting starts it too. A process that only shows a session another one drives opens it with `readOnly: true`: open recovers nothing, and every write, `resume()`, and every call that would run tasks rejects with `ReadOnlySession`. That option covers the Harness, not the storage open before it: open JSONL storage with `openNodeJsonlStorage(directory, context, { readOnly: true })` too, since a writable JSONL open repairs files the writer may be appending to (see [Storage](#storage)). SQLite storage opens as usual: SQLite's file locks keep it safe beside the writer. Each conversation has its own persisted UUIDv7 in `pi.provider`, forwarded to pi-ai as `sessionId` for provider prompt-cache and session affinity. It survives reopen, retries, reset, compaction, and model changes; a child or fork receives a fresh identity. A legacy conversation receives and persists one before its first generation or compaction request.\n" +
    '\n' +
    'A retried submission with the same `requestId` returns the existing submission instead of submitting twice:\n' +
    '\n' +
    '```typescript\n' +
    'const submission = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "Hello", requestId: "greeting-1" }, context);\n' +
    '// After a restart: the same request ID finds the same submission.\n' +
    'const again = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "Hello", requestId: "greeting-1" }, context);\n' +
    '// again.id === submission.id\n' +
    '```\n' +
    '\n' +
    '`harness.submission(id)` reacquires a submission by ID, for example to wait for it after a restart.\n' +
    '\n' +
    '### Sleeping and Waking Up\n' +
    '\n' +
    'A task waits for time by ending its phase asleep. The sleep is stored, so the task holds no invocation meanwhile, survives restarts, and resumes at the checkpoint once the Harness clock reaches `until`:\n' +
    '\n' +
    '```typescript\n' +
    'const Reminder = defineTask<{ text: string; at: number }, { phase: "wait" } | { phase: "deliver" }, null>({\n' +
    '\tname: "app.reminder",\n' +
    '\tversion: 1,\n' +
    '\tinitial: () => ({ phase: "wait" }),\n' +
    '\tphases: {\n' +
    '\t\t// Resolves once the sleep is stored; the phase ends there.\n' +
    '\t\twait: (task, runtime, context) => runtime.sleepUntil(task.input.at, { phase: "deliver" }, context),\n' +
    '\t\tdeliver: async (task, runtime, context) => {\n' +
    '\t\t\tawait notify(task.input.text);\n' +
    '\t\t\tawait runtime.commit(() => ({ status: "terminal", outcome: { status: "completed", result: null } }), context);\n' +
    '\t\t},\n' +
    '\t},\n' +
    '\tabort: (_task, runtime, context) =>\n' +
    '\t\truntime.commit(() => ({ status: "terminal", outcome: { status: "aborted" } }), context),\n' +
    '});\n' +
    '```\n' +
    '\n' +
    'There is no sleep in the middle of a phase: a phase reruns from its top after a restart, so work after the wait goes in the next phase, and what it needs goes in the checkpoint. `{ status: "sleeping", until, checkpoint }` returned from `runtime.commit()` is the same sleep, committed together with other writes; with `signals` it also wakes on a signal (see [Signals](#signals)), and `until` becomes optional. Retry backoffs and deferred-response polls of the built-in tasks sleep the same way.\n' +
    '\n' +
    'The timers of the Session, the sc',
  env: '\n' +
    '## Environment\n' +
    '\n' +
    "`env` builds the execution environment for each tool call, section rendering, and `runtime.env()`. It receives the conversation's ID, its agent `cwd`, and committed reads, so one function serves a directory per conversation or a container per conversation:\n" +
    '\n' +
    '```typescript\n' +
    'import { NodeExecutionEnv } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/env/node";\n' +
    '\n' +
    'const harness = await Harness.open(storage, {\n' +
    '\tmodels,\n' +
    '\tregistry,\n' +
    '\tenv: ({ cwd }) => new NodeExecutionEnv({ cwd: cwd ?? process.cwd() }),\n' +
    '}, context);\n' +
    '```\n' +
    '\n' +
    "A throw from `env` becomes the call's error result. Without an environment, the built-in tools fail with an error result. A fresh environment object per call is fine: `edit` and `write` serialize changes to one file by the environment's `id` and path. A custom `ExecutionEnv` sets `id` so that equal ids see the same files at the same paths, for example one id per container.\n" +
    '\n' +
    "Hosts can use the environment directly too, for example to show a project's files. `openBinaryReader()` reads byte ranges of one opened file, `openDirReader()` pages a directory, and `exec()` with an argv array runs a program without a shell, reporting which stream each output chunk came from:\n" +
    '\n' +

https://lucumr.pocoo.org/feed.atom Armin Ronacher's Thoughts and Writings Armin Ronacher's personal blog about programming, games and random thoughts that come to his mind. en 2026-11-23T10:31:40.586470+00:00 Armin Ronacher https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/11/9/irontown/ AI and Irontown 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00 Armin Ronacher For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.

A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.

The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns. He doesn’t take sides, but he wants to understand and find the truth. Another character is San (whom they call Mononoke), a girl who was raised by wolves and, despite being human, considers herself part of the forest.

This movie’s backdrop is human progress, and it reminded me so much of the challenges we are facing today with AI. AI is useful, empowering and consequential beyond the people who benefit from it. It’s similar to the iron in the story. Irontown gives the outcast purpose and power. There are people today who see themselves in an environment just like that: people who were never let in before and who can now build things that were out of reach. They are wielding AI to their benefit. But there are negative externalities. In Mononoke it’s not just the spirits and animals in the forest who bear the consequences, it’s also other people. Irontown produces guns, and its people are engaged in fights with other humans. There is conflict and power seeking everywhere.

Another, unseen character is the power-hungry emperor, who wants the head of the forest spirit, a god, because he believes it will make him immortal. Eboshi is willing to support that cause, not because she thinks it’s right, but because she is at war with the forest’s gods who are preventing her expansion, so they have a common interest. But there really is no need for anyone to kill the forest spirit, in the same way there is no need for any one country to “win at AI”. What drives it is the fear of what happens if someone else wins first. And the emperor is willing to have a god killed for it. The people who help him with that desire, Eboshi included, don’t understand the chaos it will unleash.

There it also shows the dangers of seeking overwhelming power without comprehension of how to control its consequences. The pursuit of power itself becomes destructive. In the end, the gods die, and what grows back is not the old forest anymore. Irontown is destroyed. Eboshi wants to rebuild it, and to build a better town this time. Ashitaka stays with the people of Irontown after his curse is lifted by the dying forest spirit. San cannot forgive the humans and stays with the wolves. In the end, nothing is truly resolved, but there is a truce that came at great cost.

Ashitaka’s role in the movie is one of a neutral actor. He was wronged both by a spirit turned demon in the forest, who put a curse on him, and, indirectly, by Eboshi, who caused the spirit to turn evil. Yet he harbors no ill will towards either side. He sets out to “see with eyes unclouded by hate,” and in the course of the movie he is seen as an unaligned actor. He helps people on both sides, and stands in their way to prevent further conflict. He doesn’t feel like a pacifist, but he’s the closest to one there is. He’s a truth seeker in a changing world. Because he engages he’s seen as suspicious by both sides, and ends up shot by the people of Irontown when he tries to rescue San.

I use AI every day and find it genuinely empowering. But I also recognize the pain it causes some, and the moral problems it poses. It’s genuine progress for humanity, but it comes at significant cost. And many of those costs will be carried by people who aren’t going to benefit from it.

So it’s no surprise that AI feels like a threat to many today. Communities currently strongly align themselves with one side and fight against the other. The forest spirit did not have to die and the boars did not have to die in a senseless war.

The question is not whether there will be iron, but what kind of Irontown we build with it. I want our conversation about AI to make room for nuance and genuine understanding, for us to look at it and each other with eyes unclouded by hate. We should take advantage of its real benefits, but also recognize the damage it can do, and the choices we still have about what we build and what we’re willing to sacrifice for it. I like to think there is a path for people with differing opinions can find a way to live alongside before losing something we can’t get back.

]]> https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/10/29/qwen3-custom-voices/ Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS 2026-10-29T00:00:00+00:00 2026-10-29T00:00:00+00:00 Armin Ronacher With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron crawler and we’re trying to learn a bit about game development along the way. However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we wanted to get a narrator and voice over.

But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which uses voice embeddings for custom voices.

With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it.

What Qwen Offers

Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We initially used Kokoro. However Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.

In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:

  • 1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
  • 1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
  • 1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description

The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.

At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.

Playing With It

For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI Conf, cut between two pauses so that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper. The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original recording.

Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother.

The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used 0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:

import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
    text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(),
    language="English",
    instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
    "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
    "aloud to a friend.",
)

You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Voice Embeddings

What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below).

Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices:

base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)


def fingerprint(path):
    prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
    return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding


def blend(a, b, t):
    a, b = a.float(), b.float()
    mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
    return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(
        torch.bfloat16
    )


armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")

Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice.

If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference:

import soundfile as sf

mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(
    open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed
)  # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")

The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file.

So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good does that work? I took an episode of State of Agentic Coding, the podcast Ben and I record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an embedding of me form the conference.

Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right.

On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For instance ECAPA, finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.

Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructed Cloned Voices

But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either (voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:

def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
    ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
    told = [
        cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0] if instruct else None
    ]
    voice = {
        "ref_code": [None],
        "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
        "x_vector_only_mode": [True],
        "icl_mode": [False],
    }
    codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
        input_ids=ids,
        instruct_ids=told,
        voice_clone_prompt=voice,
        languages=[language],
        non_streaming_mode=True,
        **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
    )
    wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
    return wavs[0], rate

    "I really thought this would work.",
    armin,
    "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.",
)

Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their game.

 Pi 1.0 | Earendil MENU Purpose Values Join Us Posts RFC Pi Radius Lefos Works Pi 1.0 Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 From: Earendil &lt; rfc@earendil.com &gt; To: You Subject: Pi 1.0 Today we are proudly shipping Pi 1.0: a hardened, minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own. Hundreds of thousands of people around the world use Pi every week. Many of you submit issues and pull requests. Over the course of many months, we have used that feedback to improve, harden and evolve Pi into a stable piece of software that people and businesses can depend on. Pi is known for being minimal. We care about holding that line. While agentic tooling changes every week, many of the changes do not last. Pi does not work that way. We wait until something has proven itself, and only then do we consider adopting it; weighing its true functionality against its inherent added complexity. We spoke more about that process and how it relates to Codemode and MCP earlier this week here . The Pi 1.0 we are shipping today is a result of that process. Pi already ran the latest models from every major provider, became a daily driver coding agent for people around the world, and provided a supermalleable substrate on which to build agentic applications. With Pi 1.0 we are adding the following into Pi: Codemode (native support for MCP, and non-LLM models like Jev and image models) Extension support for virtual models Deferred tool loading Cache warming for anthropic models Mid-conversation system messages (transcript-aware prompt and tool changes) A new TUI theme Full-screen mode by default We have thought about many of these features for months. They were thrown up against the wall and stuck. The list of things that fell off the wall is much longer. When we use Pi with all these new features it feels like a major step forward, but it also still feels simple, like Pi. Alongside this work of continually refining and evolving Pi, we also began to understand that there were aspects of Pi that did not fit the shape of how many people wanted to use it. At Earendil, we want to bring Pi's minimalism and the way it allows you to wield AI outside of the coding agent and outside of the terminal. It needs to be reachable from different surfaces and support longer-running conversations and tasks. In short, Pi must become more durable. Rather than stray from our minimal roots and try to make Pi something it wasn't, we combined that work into a new experimental package that we are shipping today, Pi Durable. Pi Durable is a new substrate for building long-running agentic applications that lets the builders and the users of those applications wield and steer the underlying intelligence with tremendous dexterity. It shares Pi's key principles, minimalism and supermalleability, but it extends those principles into new dimensions. Mario writes in more detail about how we crafted Pi Durable here . Earendil was formed to craft software and open protocols that strengthen human agency. Today we are shipping tools to you all to help do just that. We're eager to hear feedback from you and to harness the future out in the open together. Pi 1.0 is available today: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh or on Windows powershell -c "irm https://pi.dev/install.ps1 | iex" Pi Durable is available today as an experimental package: npm install @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/chord Both are MIT licensed. Documentation is at pi.dev . Code is at github.com/ear

# Pi

Pi is a minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own.

Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around. Customize Pi with [extensions](docs/extensions.md), [skills](docs/skills.md), [prompt templates](docs/prompt-templates.md), and [themes](docs/themes.md). Bundle them as [Pi packages](docs/packages.md) and share via npm or git.

Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub-agents and plan mode. Ask Pi to build what you want, or install a package that does it your way.

Use Pi [interactively](docs/usage.md), automate it in [print or JSON mode](docs/cli.md), control it over [RPC](docs/rpc.md), or build apps with the [Pi TypeScript SDK](docs/sdk.md). See [OpenClaw](https://github.com/OpenClaw/OpenClaw) for a real-world integration.

## Getting started

Install the command-line interface:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows:

```shell
powershell -c "irm https://pi.dev/install.ps1 | iex"
```

The installer pins all dependencies and updates Pi with `pi update`. Alternativ</result>

# Pi Durable (`@earendil-works/pi-durable`): report

Today is 2026-11-23. All facts below come from primary sources unless marked otherwise. I ran no trial; everything is read from source and documentation.

Two corrections to the premise:
- The announcement is dated 2026-10-01 and was published together with Pi 1.0.
- I found no Cloudflare-authored post. "pi-durable on Cloudflare" is the Earendil repo `earendil-works/pi-durable-cloudflare`.

## 1. What it is

- Pi Durable is an experimental harness framework for long-running, durable agents that run anywhere there is a JavaScript runtime. The announcement says it "does not replace the Pi coding agent". It is a framework for building any agentic application, coding agents included. (docs: https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/ and https://earendil.com/posts/pi-1-0/)
- Version: 1.6.0, released 2026-11-20 (npm registry, https://registry.npmjs.org/@earendil-works/pi-durable). It is MIT licensed and the repo was pushed on 2026-11-23. The README says "Experimental. The API changes without notice between releases." (source: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/durable)
- Pi packages it reuses:
  - It depends on `@earendil-works/pi-ai` for model access, which is the same package the coding agent uses.
  - It depends on `@earendil-works/chord` (document state and operations), `pi-schema`, `pi-codemode` and `pi-telemetry`.
  - The announcement says it shares the coding agent's TUI components in the demos.
- What it replaces or bypasses: the package list has no `pi-agent-core`. Durable has its own `Harness`, task scheduler and storage layer. It ships its own read, write, edit and bash tools (`CodingTools`). The announcement shows no use of `pi-coding-agent`; its demos live inside that package under `experimental/`, borrowing its TUI.

## 2. Architecture

- **Terms** (announcement):
  - Harness: storage plus the machinery to run conversations in parallel.
  - Conversation: a transcript of immutable entries.
  - Agent: a model plus its settings and tools.
  - Task: everything the harness runs, from model calls to tool calls.
  - Execution environment: where tools do their work.
- **Where the loop runs.** In the process that owns the storage. "One process owns a storage at a time, and other clients attach to that process." There is no cross-process locking (README, Storage). Read-only viewers can open the same storage with `readOnly: true`.
- **State and persistence.**
  - Every change goes through atomic commits. Nothing is shown before its commit is stored. A commit can write entries, documents and tasks together.
  - Documents are typed JSON next to the transcript. Built-in documents are `pi.agent`, `pi.live`, `pi.inbox`, `pi.usage` and `pi.provider`.
  - Storage backends are memory, IndexedDB, SQLite, JSONL and a Cloudflare Durable Object SQLite backend.
  - SQLite uses WAL with `synchronous = NORMAL`. Commits survive process crashes, but the newest may be lost on power or host failure.
  - JSONL keeps the whole history in memory, so the README says to use SQLite for long-running agents.
  - Older messages always stay in storage, even after compaction.
- **Crash recovery.**
  - Each task is a durable state machine that saves a checkpoint at every step. A new process opens the storage, finds unfinished tasks and calls `harness.resume()`.
  - A cut-off model request is re-sent, and the partial answer stays in the transcript marked aborted. A request that keeps killing the process eventually ends.
  - A cut-off tool call reruns only if the tool declares `replay: "safe"`. Otherwise the model is told the call was interrupted, along with the output stored so far.
  - A `requestId` on a submission makes it exactly-once.
  - Hooks that make decisions store them in a `memo`, where the first write wins.
- **Tool execution.**
  - Each tool call is its own task, and its intent is stored before it runs.
  - Tools reach files and shell through an `ExecutionEnv`. The `env` function runs per tool call, so each conversation can use a different directory, container, remote VM or in-memory sandbox.
  - Shipped: `NodeExecutionEnv` for local files. The README mentions pi-env's `RemoteExecutionEnv` and `LocalExecutionEnv`.
  - Codemode runs model-written JavaScript in a QuickJS sandbox (`pi-codemode`) that can also resume after a restart. On Cloudflare you pass a `RemoteCodemodeSandbox`.
  - The README does not document a built-in permission or approval system. The announcement shows an approval hook written as an extension (blocks `deploy`, asks in Slack).
- **Client connection.**
  - `conversation.watch()` returns the current view first, then each commit as Chord operations. These are "small enough to send over a socket", and you wire the transport yourself.
  - `watchEvents()` converts commits into the coding agent's event shapes, at the cost of more bytes on the wire.
  - The view holds a window of the newest 50 entries. `ConversationTranscript` handles reconnects and "load earlier".
  - A late-joining or reconnecting client starts from the current view.
  - I found no standard wire protocol. The Cloudflare example defines its own in `src/protocol.ts`.
- **Background and long-running work.**
  - Tasks are foreground by default, so Esc or an abort stops them and everything they own.
  - A background task (`ownership: { kind: "conversation" }, background: true`) lets the conversation go idle while it runs, and an ordinary abort leaves it alone. The announcement gives a subagent and a reminder that fires tomorrow as examples.
  - Tasks and conversations form one ownership tree, and aborts run bottom-up.
  - Sleeps are stored (`runtime.sleepUntil`) and hold no invocation while waiting.
  - Compaction is a task that runs in the background while the conversation continues. `reset()` and handoff start a new context.
  - Subagents are not built in. A tool creates a child conversation it owns.
- **Multiple clients and conversations.**
  - Any number of clients can attach to any conversation, and any client can steer.
  - Submitting to a busy conversation queues it in `pi.inbox`. `whenBusy: "steer"` joins the running work after the current tool round. A follow-up starts the next run.
  - One harness runs many conversations concurrently. A conversation can fork at any entry and sees the parent's history without copying it.

## 3. Differences from pi-coding-agent

The coding-agent side comes from https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/coding-agent and the Pi 1.0 post. I did not re-verify the JSONL session tree or the four-tool default in the coding-agent docs, so those items are your premise, not confirmed here.

| Aspect | Pi coding agent | Pi Durable (source) |
|---|---|---|
| Process model | "Runs on your (remote) machine, inside a terminal, driven by one person. If the process dies, you look at what happened and tell it to continue." | Process death is resumed automatically from checkpoints. Multiple humans can steer the same agents. |
| Session state | Your premise: JSONL tree | Entries, documents and tasks in pluggable storage (SQLite, Durable Object, etc.) with atomic commits. JSONL is one optional backend. Forks share parent history. |
| Core package | `pi-agent-core` loop | A separate `Harness` and task scheduler. |
| Tools | Your premise: four tools | Built-ins are `CodingTools` (read, write, edit, bash), plus codemode and tool search. Each conversation selects its own tool set. Each call is a durable task with a `replay` declaration. |
| Extensions | Your premise: in-process, full permissions | An extension is a named bundle of prompt sections, tools, hooks, tasks and documents. Conversations store extension names, never code. Extensions can be hot-replaced without stopping the agent. Hooks participate in durability. |
| UI | TUI (`pi-tui`) | No UI is built in. UIs attach through `watch()`. Demos reuse the coding agent's TUI components. |
| Subagents | The coding-agent README says it skips them | Not built in. A few lines of tool code build one. |
| Where tools run | Local machine | The execution-environment interface allows the harness on one machine and tools on another. |

## 4. Stated trade-offs

- **Gains** (announcement): runs anywhere, long conversations through compaction, crash survival, multi-client steering, and malleability. The source is about 15,000 lines without tests, which Earendil gives as about 150k to 250k tokens, so an agent can read it.
- **Costs and limits** (stated):
  - It is experimental and the API may change.
  - One process owns a storage, with no cross-process locking.
  - Recovery re-sends cut-off model requests, which costs tokens.
  - Non-idempotent tools must be written with replay semantics in mind. A tool without `replay: "safe"` is never rerun after a crash.
  - A phase reruns from its top after a restart, so work after a wait must go in the next phase.
  - SQLite can lose the newest commits on power or host failure.
  - The `watchEvents()` compatibility layer costs more bytes than operations.
  - Storage conformance suites and benchmarks ship in the package, but I found no published latency numbers.
- **Not documented:** latency overhead, a security or permission model, and infrastructure cost comparisons. The announcement does not name them as trade-offs. The Cloudflare sample says it has "no authentication or rate limiting" and warns to add both before exposing a deployment.

## 5. Cloudflare deployment

Source: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-durable-cloudflare, repo pushed 2026-11-10, depends on pi-durable 1.5.2.
- One SQLite-backed Durable Object class, `Session`, holds the harness. Commits are DO storage transactions (`openDurableObjectSqliteStorage(ctx.storage)`). The README states that "multiple Pi storages opened through the Cloudflare adapter with the same storage object automatically share an operation queue."
- Wake-up after eviction uses the `onWake` option. The harness arms no timers, and the host keeps a DO alarm armed from `harness.wake()` and calls `resume()` when it fires. The sample keeps a 60-second heartbeat alarm while work can run.
- Clients connect over Cloudflare hibernating WebSockets. Each socket watches one conversation, receiving a first value and then Chord operations. A React client applies them. Each connection is tagged with a username for multiplayer.
- The sample has features for forks, scheduled and recurring follow-ups, a search subagent, and an Activity view of live task ownership.
- There is no Cloudflare Sandbox or container in the sample. I found no `env` or Sandbox usage in `src/chat.ts`, and `wrangler.jsonc` binds only the Durable Object. The pi-durable README mentions only `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` for Cloudflare. Remote tool execution is possible through the `ExecutionEnv` interface but is not demonstrated.
- `wrangler.jsonc` enables observability and traces. The package emits telemetry spans (`pi.durable.phase`, etc.) through `pi-telemetry`.
